sections.heading: The Constitution's legal skeleton — a lawyer's summary

blocks.text: This law-unit theme re-reads the polity notes through a **legal lens**: the Constitution as **supreme law** (Art 13 voiding inconsistent laws), its **nature** (written, quasi-federal, parliamentary, justiciable rights), and the **rights-directives architecture** as enforceable vs aspirational law. What the examiner wants here is the LEGAL operation — which provision, what remedy, which court.

headers: Fundamental Rights (Part III) — the enforceable core
rows: **Art 14** equality
Reasonable-classification test (intelligible differentia + rational nexus); arbitrariness doctrine (**Royappa**); the manifest-arbitrariness ground (**Shayara Bano, 2017** — triple talaq struck)
**Art 19** six freedoms
Citizens only; each freedom with its own reasonable-restriction clause (19(2)-(6)); proportionality review post-**Puttaswamy**
**Arts 20-22** criminal-process rights

No ex-post-facto, double jeopardy, self-incrimination (20); life-liberty by fair procedure (21 — the residuary rights mine: privacy, dignity, speedy trial); arrest safeguards + preventive-detention limits (22)
Anti-exploitation (trafficking, child labour); religious freedom with public-order caps; minority culture-education rights (**TMA Pai's** framework)
**Art 32** remedies
The right TO enforce rights — five writs; 'the soul' (Ambedkar); HCs' Art 226 wider (any purpose)
**DPSPs (Part IV)**

Non-justiciable duties of the State (39's distributive clauses, 39A legal aid, 43 living wage, 44 UCC, 48A environment) — judicially fused with FRs (**Minerva Mills'** balance doctrine); the FR-DPSP harmonisation is basic structure

sections.heading: Centre-state division of powers — the legal machinery

items: **Legislative division** (Arts 245-254; Seventh Schedule): the three lists with Union predominance; doctrines the courts police with — **pith & substance, colourable legislation, repugnancy (254), harmonious construction** (the PC-005 file, here cited as case law: Balsara, Gajapati, Karunanidhi).

**Administrative & financial division**: Arts 256-263 (directions, delegation, Inter-State Council), Arts 268-293 (taxing heads' separation — no overlap by design; GST's 246A concurrency the exception; borrowing limits 293(3) — the AP-relevant consent requirement while indebted to the Centre).

**The legal character question**: 'Indian federalism is a legal hierarchy with political negotiation' — Bommai's judicial review of 356, Art 131 suits (state-vs-Centre litigation: AP's own water/asset suits context), and the **Art 143 advisory** channel — federal disputes are justiciable in India to a degree rare among federations.
**Answer craft**: for this theme, always answer with **provision + doctrine + case** triplets; the polity-note content (PC-001/002/005) supplies substance — the law lens supplies the marks.

items: Differentiate from the polity notes by register: legal operation and remedy, not institutional description.

blocks.text: Exam tip: In the law unit, every assertion earns its mark only with its provision number attached — write like a junior counsel, not a commentator.

prelimsPointers: **Art 13**: 'law' includes ordinance, order, bye-law, rule, custom — all void to the extent of FR inconsistency.
**Art 21's expansion**: Maneka (1978) — procedure must be just-fair-reasonable; progeny — privacy (Puttaswamy 2017), speedy trial (Hussainara), shelter, environment.
**Writ literacy**: habeas corpus (detention), mandamus (public duty), prohibition & certiorari (jurisdictional control), quo warranto (office's title).
**Art 20** protections apply even in emergency (44th Amendment's non-derogables with 21).
**Doctrine of severability & eclipse** — Art 13's operational doctrines (RMDC; Bhikaji Narain).
**Art 293(3)**: a state indebted to the Centre needs central consent to borrow — the fiscal-federal leash.
**TMA Pai (2002)** — 11-judge framework on minority educational rights (Art 30).
mainsAngles: Read Parts III and IV as one charter — enforceable liberty and directed welfare fused by judicial balance.
Article 21 became the residuary right — trace its expansion and the discipline proportionality now imposes.
The Seventh Schedule is policed by doctrine — illustrate pith-and-substance, colourability and repugnancy with cases.
Indian federal disputes are justiciable — evaluate Articles 131, 143 and Bommai as the legal machinery of federalism.
Write the provision-doctrine-case method: demonstrate it on equality, liberty and repugnancy questions.

glossary.definition: Art 14's test — a valid differentia rationally connected to the law's object; arbitrariness its modern supplement.
Art 21's standard read to require fair, just and reasonable procedure — due process in substance.
Only the unconstitutional part of a law falls if separable — Art 13's scalpel.
Pre-constitutional laws inconsistent with FRs are dormant, not dead — revived if the inconsistency is removed.
Concurrent-field conflict resolved for Union law (Art 254), saving assented state laws.
Art 143 — Presidential references for the SC's opinion; federalism's consultative valve.

sections.heading: Powers of the three organs — the legal inventory

rows: **Legislature**

Law-making within lists; constituent power (368); financial control (no tax/spend without it — Arts 265/266); oversight devices; privileges (105/194); impeachment-removal powers (President, judges); delegated-legislation grants
Judicial review (competence + FRs + basic structure); presidential returns; bicameral checks; election accountability
**Executive**

Aid-advice governance (74/163); ordinance power (123/213 — legislative in nature, judicially disciplined: **Krishna Kumar Singh**); delegated legislation (rules-notifications — the modern statute's bulk); treaty-making; pardons (72/161 — **judicially reviewable: Epuru Sudhakar, an AP case**); appointments; emergency powers
Legislative responsibility (75(3)); judicial review of action (14's arbitrariness; proportionality); CAG audit; no-confidence
**Judiciary**

Judicial review (the trinity: legislation, action, amendments); writ jurisdiction; contempt power (129/215); rule-making for courts; **Art 142's complete-justice** power (the elastic clause — Ayodhya, TN Governor's deemed assent — with its overreach debate); guideline-legislation in vacuums (**Vishaka doctrine**)

Appointment-removal process; legislative override by valid re-enactment (curing the defect); Art 121/211 speech bars; self-restraint doctrines (political-question avoidance, presumption of constitutionality)

sections.heading: Separation of powers — the Indian doctrine

items: **Not Montesquieu's wall but functional distribution**: India separates **functions with overlaps** (ordinances = executive legislation; tribunals = executive adjudication; contempt = judicial punishment) — the doctrine's Indian formulation: no organ may **usurp the essential function** of another (**Ram Jawaya Kapur, 1955**; separation as basic structure — **Indira Nehru Gandhi, 1975**, striking the election-dispute clause).

**The friction files**: judicial legislation (Vishaka's defence: interim gap-filling vs the criticism of mandamus-governance); legislative overruling of judgments (permissible only by **removing the basis**, not by declaring a judgment void — **Cauvery reference; Madras Bar Assn** line); executive's tribunal control (the Madras Bar Association series policing composition); Art 142's widening (the 2025-era Presidential-reference debate on assent timelines — PC-004's file, cited here as the separation question it is).

**The balanced close**: Indian separation is a **dialogue of checks** — each organ holding elastic powers, each disciplined by the others' review; the health test is not purity of separation but **accountability at each overlap**.

flowchart TD
  A[Separation - functional, not absolute] --> B[Legislature: laws, purse, constituent power]
  A --> C[Executive: ordinances, rules, pardons, appointments]
  A --> D[Judiciary: review, writs, Art 142, contempt]
  B --> E[Overlap: delegated legislation to executive]
  C --> F[Overlap: ordinance legislation]
  D --> G[Overlap: Vishaka-type guidelines]
  E --> H[Check: laying procedure, review]
  F --> H
  G --> H
  H --> I[Essential-function usurpation barred - Ram Jawaya, basic structure]

items: The three-row inventory + the functional-separation doctrine + two friction files = complete; **Epuru Sudhakar (AP)** on pardons and Krishna Kumar Singh on ordinances are the precision citations.
'Accountability at each overlap' is the evaluative standard to end on.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Ram Jawaya (1955) for the doctrine, Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975) for its basic-structure status — the two-case spine of every separation answer; Art 142's current controversies supply the freshness.

prelimsPointers: **Ram Jawaya Kapur (1955)** — Indian separation is functional; no organ may usurp another's essential function.
**Separation of powers held part of the basic structure** in Indira Nehru Gandhi (1975).
**Ordinances**: Arts 123/213; lapse 6 weeks after reassembly; re-promulgation a fraud (Krishna Kumar Singh, 2017).
**Pardons reviewable**: **Epuru Sudhakar v. Govt of AP (2006)** — relevant/irrelevant-considerations review of Art 161 clemency.
**Art 142** — 'complete justice' power unique to the SC; instrument of the Ayodhya decree and the 2025 assent controversies.
**Vishaka (1997)** — judicial guidelines valid as interim law until legislation (the gap-filling doctrine).
Legislatures may nullify a judgment's **basis** by valid retrospective law, but cannot simply overrule the judgment.
mainsAngles: Functional distribution, not watertight separation — expound the Indian doctrine from Ram Jawaya to the basic-structure holding.
Each organ legislates a little, judges a little, executes a little — audit the overlaps and their accountability devices.
Article 142 is equity with a constitution-sized jurisdiction — debate its use from Ayodhya to assent timelines.
When may Parliament undo a judgment? State the removing-the-basis doctrine with cases.
Tribunalisation tests separation at the executive-judicial seam — evaluate with the Madras Bar Association line.

glossary.definition: The Indian separation rule — organs may share functions but none may take over another's core role.
Rules-regulations made by the executive under statutory authority — the modern statute's operative bulk, checked by laying and review.
Executive-made temporary law during legislative recess (123/213) — subject to placement, lapse and judicial discipline.
The SC's power to pass any decree needed for full justice in a cause — equity's constitutional residuary.
The only valid legislative response to an adverse judgment — curing the defect the court found, prospectively or retrospectively.
Court-made norms (Vishaka guidelines) filling statutory vacuums — defended as interim, criticised as trespass.

sections.heading: The court pyramid — civil and criminal sides

rows: Apex
**Supreme Court** — appeals (SLP 136; civil 133), original (131), advisory (143)
Same court — criminal appeals (134), death-confirmation ultimately
State
**High Court** — first/second appeals, writs (226), superintendence (227), original civil side in some HCs
Criminal appeals-revisions; **death sentences require HC confirmation (Sec 407 BNSS/366 CrPC lineage)**
District
**District Judge** (the principal civil court; also hears appeals from munsiff-level); Additional DJs; commercial courts at this tier
**Sessions Judge** (same officer wearing the criminal robe) — tries offences committed to sessions (7+ yr punishments); can pass any sentence, **death subject to HC confirmation**
Below
**Senior Civil Judge → Junior Civil Judge (munsiff)** — pecuniary jurisdiction ladders (state-set)

**Chief Judicial Magistrate (up to 7 yrs) → Judicial Magistrate First Class (up to 3 yrs/fine) → JMSC**; Metropolitan Magistrates in metros; Executive Magistrates (preventive, not trial, functions — the DM's side)
Base & alternatives
**Gram Nyayalayas** (mobile village courts, 2008 Act), Lok Adalats (award = decree; no appeal), tribunals (specialised), arbitration-mediation (**Mediation Act 2023**)
Same Nyayalayas (petty criminal); plea bargaining (2005-added, now BNSS chapter)

sections.heading: Substantive vs procedural law — the classification that organises everything

items: **Substantive law defines rights-duties-offences**: what murder IS (**BNS 2023**, replacing IPC), what a contract IS (Contract Act 1872), property (TPA 1882), torts (uncodified) — the WHAT of law.

**Procedural (adjective) law enforces them**: HOW to try — **BNSS 2023** (replacing CrPC) for criminal process (FIR-investigation-cognizance-trial-appeal), **CPC 1908** for civil process (plaint-written statement-issues-evidence-decree-execution), **Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam 2023** (evidence — spanning both sides).

**Why the distinction matters legally**: procedure is generally **retrospective** (no vested right in procedure), substance prospective (Art 20(1)'s ex-post-facto bar for offences); procedural default can be cured, substantive illegality cannot; interpretation canons differ (procedure construed to advance justice).

**The 2023 recodification** (the currency layer): **BNS-BNSS-BSA (in force 1 July 2024)** — community service as punishment, organised-crime & terrorism as general offences, timelines (charges in 60 days, judgment in 45 post-trial), e-FIR & Zero FIR statutory, forensic mandate (7-yr+ offences), trials-in-absentia for absconders, sedition recast as 152 BNS ('acts endangering sovereignty') — modernisation with civil-liberty debates (police custody extension, 152's breadth) to note on both sides.

items: Draw the pyramid with the dual-hat district tier (DJ = Sessions Judge); sentence-power ladder (JMFC 3 yrs → CJM 7 → Sessions any, death needing HC confirmation) is the precision set.
Substantive-vs-procedural: definition pair + retrospectivity rule + the 2023 recodification's five features with one critique.

blocks.text: Exam tip: 'The District Judge and the Sessions Judge are one officer with two jurisdictions' — the line that shows you know the pyramid from inside; the BNS-BNSS-BSA feature-set is 2024-26's guaranteed currency question.

prelimsPointers: Sentence powers: **JMFC — up to 3 years; CJM — up to 7; Sessions — any sentence, death subject to High Court confirmation**.
**District Judge (civil) and Sessions Judge (criminal) are the same officer** — Arts 233-237 govern the cadre.
**Gram Nyayalayas Act 2008** — mobile village courts (Nyayadhikari = JMFC rank); Lok Adalat awards are **deemed decrees, non-appealable**.
**Substantive**: BNS 2023, Contract Act 1872, TPA 1882; **Procedural**: BNSS 2023, CPC 1908; **BSA 2023** (evidence) — new codes in force **1 July 2024**.
Procedure applies **retrospectively** (no vested right in procedure); **Art 20(1)** bars retrospective offences/penalties.
BNSS features: **e-FIR/Zero FIR statutory, forensics mandatory for 7-yr+ offences, judgment within 45 days of trial-end, trial in absentia**.
**Sedition (124A IPC) recast as Sec 152 BNS** — 'acts endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India'.
**Mediation Act 2023** institutionalised pre-litigation mediation; plea bargaining continues under BNSS.
mainsAngles: Map the civil and criminal court pyramids and the one officer who anchors both at the district.
Distinguish substantive from procedural law and show why the distinction decides retrospectivity and cure.
Audit the 2023 criminal-code recodification — modernisations, timelines and the civil-liberty debates.
Justice at the base — evaluate Gram Nyayalayas, Lok Adalats and the Mediation Act as the pyramid's foundations.
Backlog is a procedure problem before a judge-strength problem — argue with case-flow and ADR evidence.

glossary.definition: A magistrate's judicial notice of an offence to set trial process in motion — the criminal case's ignition.
The magistrate's transfer of sessions-triable offences to the Sessions Court — the pyramid's escalator.
Law defining rights, duties and offences (BNS, contract, property) — the WHAT.
Law prescribing enforcement machinery and process (BNSS, CPC, evidence) — the HOW; generally retrospective.
FIR registrable at any police station regardless of jurisdiction, transferred later — statutory under BNSS.
Negotiated guilty plea for reduced sentence in eligible offences — docket-relief with safeguards.
